chunks.en: Insecticide resistance: Resistance to insecticides may be defined as 'a heritable change in the sensitivity of a pest population that is reflected in the repeated failure of a product to achieve the expected level of control when used according to the label recommendation for that pest species' (IRAC). Cross-resistance occurs when resistance to one insecticide confers resistance to another insecticide, even where the insect has not been exposed to the latter product.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, p.72

chunks.en: Causes of resistance development: The causes and rate at which insecticide resistance develops depend on several factors, including the initial frequency of resistance alleles present in the population, how rapidly the insects reproduce, the insects' level of resistance, the migration and host range of the insects, the insecticide's persistence and specificity, and the rate, timing and number of applications of insecticide made.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, p.72

chunks.en: For instance, insect pests that survive in large populations and breed quickly are at greater advantage of evolving insecticide, especially when insecticides are misused or over-used. The best strategy to avoid insecticide resistance is prevention and including insecticide resistance management tactics as part of a larger integrated pest management (IPM) approach.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, p.72

chunks.en: Monitor pests: Monitor insect population development in fields to determine if and when control measures are warranted. Monitor and consider natural enemies when making control decisions. After treatment, continue monitoring to assess pest populations and their control.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 1, p.72

chunks.en: Focus on AESA. Insecticides should be used only as a last resort when all other non-chemical management options are exhausted and P: D ratio is above 2: 1. Apply biopesticides/chemical insecticides judiciously after observing unfavourable P: D ratio and when the pests are in most vulnerable life stage. Use application rates and intervals as per label claim.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 2, p.73

chunks.en: Ecological engineering for pest management: Flowering plants that attract natural enemies as well as plants that repel pests can be grown as border/intercrop. Take an integrated approach to managing pests. Use as many different control measures as possible viz., cultural, mechanical, physical, biological etc.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 3-4, p.73

chunks.en: Select insecticides with care and consider the impact on future pest populations and the environment. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides when a narrow-spectrum or more specific insecticide will work. More preference should be given to green labeled insecticides.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 4, p.73

chunks.en: Mix and apply carefully. While applying insecticides care should be taken for proper application of insecticides in terms of dose, volume, timing, coverage, application techniques as per label claim.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 5, p.73

chunks.en: Alternate different insecticide classes. Avoid the repeated use of the same insecticide, insecticides in the same chemical class, or insecticides in different classes with same mode of action and rotate/alternate insecticide classes and modes of action.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 6, p.73

chunks.en: Preserve susceptible genes. Preserve susceptible individuals within the target population by providing unsprayed areas within treated fields, adjacent "refuge" fields, or habitat attractions within a treated field that facilitate immigration. These susceptible individuals may outcompete and interbreed with resistant individuals, diluting the resistant genes and therefore the impact of resistance.
chunks.locator: X. Insecticide resistance and its management, general strategy 7, p.73

chunks.en: Nitrogen: Under N deficiency, older leaves gradually change from green to paler green. As the deficiency progresses these older leaves become uniformly yellow (chlorotic). Leaves approach a yellowish white color under extreme deficiency.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, nitrogen, p.73

chunks.en: Nitrogen: The young leaves at the top of the plant maintain a green but paler color and tend to become smaller in size. Branching is reduced resulting in short, spindly plants. The yellowing in nitrogen deficiency is uniform over the entire leaf including the veins.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, nitrogen, p.73

chunks.en: Nitrogen deficiency - Correction Measure: Recovery can be done by top dressing of urea of as recommended on soil test basis or apply 2 % urea solution. Recovery of deficient plants to applied nitrogen is immediate (days) and spectacular.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, nitrogen, correction measure, p.73

chunks.en: Phosphorus: The symptoms first develop on older leaves showing some necrotic spots and plants are dwarfed or stunted. Phosphorus deficient plants develop very slowly. Plants develop a distinct purpling of the stem, petiole and the under sides of the leaves. Under severe deficiency conditions there is a tendency for leaves to develop a blue-gray luster.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, phosphorus, p.73-74

chunks.en: Phosphorus deficiency - Correction Measure: Soil application of recommended dose of phosphorous should be applied at the time of sowing or planting.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, phosphorus, correction measure, p.73-74

chunks.en: Potassium: Since potassium is very mobile within the plant, symptoms only develop on young leaves in the case of extreme deficiency. Some of the leaves show marginal necrosis (tip burn), and at a more advanced deficiency status show inter-veinal necrosis. This group of symptoms is very characteristic of K deficiency symptoms.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, potassium, p.74

chunks.en: Potassium: As the deficiency progresses, most of the interveinal area becomes necrotic, the veins remain green and the leaves tend to curl and crinkle. In contrast to nitrogen deficiency, chlorosis is irreversible in potassium deficiency, even if potassium is given to the plants.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, potassium, p.74

chunks.en: Potassium deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar application of K2SO4 @1%.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, potassium, correction measure, p.74

chunks.en: Sulfur: This leaves show a general overall chlorosis. The veins and petioles show a very distinct reddish color. The yellowing is much more uniform over the entire plant including young leaves. The reddish color often found on the underside of the leaves. With advanced sulfur deficiency the leaves tend to become more erect and often twisted and brittle.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, sulfur, p.74

chunks.en: Sulfur deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of K2SO4 or CaSO4 1% twice at fortnightly interval.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, sulfur, correction measure, p.74

chunks.en: Magnesium: The Mg-deficient leaves show advanced interveinal chlorosis, In its advanced form, magnesium deficiency may superficially resemble potassium deficiency. The symptoms generally start with mottled chlorotic areas developing in the interveinal tissue.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, magnesium, p.74

chunks.en: Magnesium deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of MgSO4 @2%.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, magnesium, correction measure, p.74

chunks.en: Manganese: The leaves show a light interveinal chlorosis developed under a limited supply of Mn. The early stages of the chlorosis induced by manganese deficiency are somewhat similar to iron deficiency. As the stress increases, the leaves develop dark necrotic areas along the veins.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, manganese, p.74

chunks.en: Manganese deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of MnSO4 @ 2%.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, manganese, correction measure, p.74

chunks.en: Molybdenum: The leaves show some mottled spotting along with some interveinal chlorosis. An early symptom for molybdenum deficiency is a general overall chlorosis, similar to the symptom for nitrogen deficiency but generally without the reddish coloration on the undersides of the leaves.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, molybdenum, p.75

chunks.en: Molybdenum deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of NaMO4 0.05% twice at weekly interval.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, molybdenum, correction measure, p.75

chunks.en: Zinc: The leaves show interveinal necrosis. In the early stages of zinc deficiency the younger leaves become yellow and pitting develops in the interveinal upper surfaces of the mature leaves. As the deficiency progress these symptoms develop into an intense interveinal necrosis but the main veins remain green, as in the symptoms of recovering iron deficiency.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, zinc, p.75

chunks.en: Zinc deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of ZnSO4 @ 0.5%.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, zinc, correction measure, p.75

chunks.en: Boron: These boron-deficient leaves show a light general chlorosis. Boron deficiency results in necrosis of meristematic tissues in the growing region, leading to loss of apical dominance and the development of a rosette condition. These deficiency symptoms are similar to those caused by calcium deficiency.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, boron, p.75

chunks.en: Boron: The leaves are unusually brittle and tend to break easily. Also, there is often a wilting of the younger leaves even under an adequate water supply, pointing to a disruption of water transport caused by boron deficiency.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, boron, p.75

chunks.en: Boron deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of borax @ 0.2%.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, boron, correction measure, p.75

chunks.en: Calcium: The calcium-deficient leaves show necrosis around the base of the leaves. The very low mobility of calcium is a major factor determining the expression of calcium deficiency symptoms in plants. Classic symptoms of calcium deficiency include blossom-end rot of tomato.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, calcium, p.75

chunks.en: Calcium: Symptoms show soft dead necrotic tissue at rapidly growing areas, which is generally related to poor translocation of calcium to the tissue rather than a low external supply of calcium. This ultimately results in the margins of the leaves growing more slowly than the rest of the leaf, causing the leaf to cup downward. Plants under chronic calcium deficiency have a much greater tendency to wilt than non-stressed plants.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, calcium, p.75

chunks.en: Calcium deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of 2% Calcium sulphate twice at weekly intervals.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, calcium, correction measure, p.75

chunks.en: Copper: The copper-deficient leaves are curled, and their petioles bend downward. Copper deficiency may be expressed as a light overall chlorosis along with the permanent loss of turgor in the young leaves. Recently matured leaves show netted, green veining with areas bleaching to a whitish gray. Some leaves develop sunken necrotic spots and have a tendency to bend downward.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, copper, p.76

chunks.en: Copper deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of 0.5% CuSO4 twice at fortnightly interval.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, copper, correction measure, p.76

chunks.en: Iron: The iron-deficient leaves show strong chlorosis at the base of the leaves with some green netting. The most common symptom for iron deficiency starts out as an interveinal chlorosis of the youngest leaves, evolves into an overall chlorosis, and ends as a totally bleached leaf.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, iron, p.76

chunks.en: Iron: Because iron has a low mobility, iron deficiency symptoms appear first on the youngest leaves. Iron deficiency is strongly associated with calcareous soils, anaerobic conditions, and it is often induced by an excess of heavy metals.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, iron, p.76

chunks.en: Iron deficiency - Correction Measure: Foliar spray of FeSO4 @ 0.5%.
chunks.locator: XI. Nutritional deficiencies, iron, correction measure, p.76

chunks.en: Blossom-end rot (BER) is caused by a localized Ca deficiency in the developing fruit. It begins with light tan, water-soaked areas that can then enlarge and turn black and leathery in appearance. Most often the problem occurs at the blossom end of the fruit.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, blossom-end rot, p.77

chunks.en: Blossom-end rot: Factors like low soil Ca, high N rates, using ammoniacal sources of N, high concentrations of soluble K and Mg in the soil, high salinity, low humidity, inadequate or excess soil moisture, damage to root system by nematodes, diseases etc. increases the BER problem.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, blossom-end rot, p.77

chunks.en: Blossom-end rot - Correction measure: Soil applications of Ca materials, proper fertilization and good water management can prevent the problem.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, blossom-end rot, p.77

chunks.en: Cat-facing is a generic term used to describe a tomato fruit that has a gross deformity and is usually not marketable. The defect is usually located on the blossom end of the fruit. The deformity is starts occurring during the formation of the flower that results in the fruit not developing normally.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, cat-face, p.77

chunks.en: Cat-face: Low temperatures, herbicide drifts, heavy thrips feeding and little leaf disease are some of the causes of cat-faced fruits. Correction measure: Varieties should be selected that historically have had little problem with cat-facing, avoiding spray drift, water logging etc. can reduce the problem.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, cat-face, p.77

chunks.en: Cracking occurs when the internal expansion is faster than the expansion of the epidermis and the epidermis splits. Varieties differ greatly in their susceptibility to cracking.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, cracking, p.78

chunks.en: Cracking - Correction measure: Control is through selecting tolerant varieties or by reducing fluctuations in soil moisture. Cracking may also be reduced by maintaining good foliage cover, since exposed fruit are more susceptible.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, cracking, p.78

chunks.en: Gray wall (blotchy ripening): Internally gray wall is characterized by dark necrotic areas usually in the vascular tissue of the outer walls. Outward symptoms show up as grayish appearance caused by partial collapse of the wall tissue; hence the term gray wall is used to describe. It typically develops on green fruit prior to harvest but can develop later.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, gray wall, p.78

chunks.en: Gray wall: Fruits affected are typically not marketable due to blotchy appearance as fruit ripens. Gray wall is more of a problem during cool and short days. There are variety differences in susceptibility. High N may increase the problem. Correction measure: Application of adequate K may reduce the problem.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, gray wall, p.78

chunks.en: Internal White Tissue: Fruit affected by this disorder usually show no outward symptoms. When ripe fruits are cut, white hard areas especially in the vascular region are present in the outer walls. Under severe conditions, fruit may also show white tissue in cross-wall and center of fruit. High temperatures during the ripening period in the field seem to trigger the symptoms. Correction measure: Application of adequate K fertilization may reduce it.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, internal white tissue, p.78

chunks.en: Irregular ripening is a fruit ripening disorder caused by feeding of nymphs of the silver leaf whitefly (Bemisia argentifolii) on the tomato foliage. Green fruit show no symptoms, but as fruit ripens, color fails to develop uniformly. Color often develops along locule walls with intermediate areas remaining green or yellow, producing a star-burst appearance. Correction measure: This disorder can be controlled if nymphs of white fly are controlled.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, irregular ripening, p.79

chunks.en: Pox and Fleck: In most cases when a fruit is affected both disorders are found together but are considered separate problems. Pox is described as small cuticular disruptions found at random on the fruit surface. Fleck, develops as small irregular shaped green spots at random on the surface of immature fruit, which becomes gold in color as fruit ripens.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, pox and fleck, p.79

chunks.en: Pox and Fleck: Fruits severely affected with pox and fleck are not marketable. Both conditions seem to be genetic in nature, the disorders only show up under certain environmental conditions. There are differences between varieties as to susceptibility to pox and fleck. Correction measure: Control is through selecting tolerant varieties.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, pox and fleck, p.79

chunks.en: Puffiness: When this problem is slight, it may be impossible to detect puffiness until fruit are cut. When fruit are cut, open cavities are observed between the seed gel area and the outer wall. Fruits are also very light in relation to size.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, puffiness, p.79

chunks.en: Puffiness: This problem is caused by any factor that affects fruit set, including inadequate pollination, fertilization, or seed development. Most common causes are too low or high temperatures during fruit set. Other factors such as high N, low light, or rainy conditions can also cause seed set problems. Correction measure: Application of balanced N doses may reduce the problem.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, puffiness, p.79-80

chunks.en: Zebra stripe can be characterized as a series of dark green spots arranged in a line from the stem end to the bloom end. At times it seems the spots coalesce together and form elongated markings. Many times the dark green areas will disappear when fruit ripens. This problem seems to be variety related. It is probably a genetic defect that only develops under certain environmental conditions. Zebra stripe may be linked to pox and fleck.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, zebra stripe, p.80

chunks.en: Zippering is described as a fruit having thin scars that extend partially or fully from the stem scar area to the blossom end. The longitudinal scar has small transverse scars along it. At times there may be open holes in the locules in addition to the zipper scar. Usually an anther that is attached to the newly forming fruit causes the zipper scar.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, zippering, p.80

chunks.en: Zippering: Some people feel that a zipper is formed when the "blooms" stick to the fruit and do not shed properly but this may not be a cause. Correction measure: The only control is to select varieties that are not prone to zippering.
chunks.locator: XI. Physiological and nutritional disorders, zippering, p.80

chunks.en: Pick tomatoes at 2-3 day intervals during warm weather and at weekly intervals during cool weather. Waiting period for all the pesticides, if any, should be observed without fail. Pick tomatoes from the plants by twisting them rather than pulling them to avoid damage.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, A. at the time of harvest, p.81

chunks.en: Fruits are generally removed from the upper portion of the plant. Vines and fruit should be completely dry when mature green fruit are harvested. Otherwise, fruit may develop sunken, blackened areas during ripening. Vine-ripes must be hand harvested every other day.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, A. at the time of harvest, p.81

chunks.en: A common recommendation for fresh market tomatoes is to harvest green matures when about 10% of the fruit on the first hand is at the breaker stage of maturity. When immature greens are picked, the eating quality is reduced even though these tomatoes can be gassed to redness with ethylene.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, A. at the time of harvest, p.81

chunks.en: But the sugar and acid content, which determine the taste of the tomato, are low, resulting in a flavour-less fruit. Mature green tomatoes develop flavour to the same extent as fruit left on the plant another 24 hours, until colour appears.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, A. at the time of harvest, p.81

chunks.en: Usually, tomatoes are packed after harvest and sent to fresh market. Otherwise, fresh market tomatoes are dropped into a water tank after harvest to clean the fruit. The improper tank procedures can spread the disease and increase storage losses.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, B. post-harvest storage, p.81

chunks.en: Disease spread can be minimized by not allowing 1) fruit to submerge deeply or to float more than one layer deep in the tank; 2) pressure from deeper submersion forces pathogen-containing water through the stem scar into the fruit; 3) removing fruit after two minutes; 4) slightly chlorinating the water; and 5) warming tank temperature to a few degrees above fruit temperature (cool water constricts the fruit, pulling in pathogens).
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, B. post-harvest storage, p.81

chunks.en: In general, the length of storage depends on the harvest stage. Mature green fruits can be stored up to 30 days at cool temperatures, e.g. 10 degree C. Ripe fruits can be kept for about a week.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, B. post-harvest storage, p.81

chunks.note: Commercial crops of fresh market tomatoes picked at the mature green stage are ripened artificially and uniformly by dipping the fruits.
chunks.locator: XII. Safety measures, B. post-harvest storage, p.81

chunks.en: Deep ploughing is to be done on bright sunny days during the months of May and June. The field should be kept exposed to sun light at least for 2-3 weeks. Do not plant or irrigate the field after ploughing, at least for 2-3 weeks, to allow desiccation of weed's bulbs and/or rhizomes of perennial weeds.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 1, p.82

chunks.en: Adopt crop rotation. Avoid growing monocrop. Grow only recommended varieties. Do not grow varieties not suitable for the season or the region.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, rows 2-3, p.82

chunks.en: Sow early in the season. Avoid late sowing as this may lead to reduced yields and incidence of white grubs and diseases.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 4, p.82

chunks.en: Always treat the seeds with approved chemicals/bio products for the control of seed borne diseases/pests. Do not use seeds without seed treatment with biocides/chemicals.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 5, p.82

chunks.en: Sow in rows at optimum depths under proper moisture conditions for better establishment. Do not sow seeds beyond 5-7 cm depth.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 6, p.82

chunks.en: Maintain optimum and healthy crop stand which would be capable of competing with weeds at a critical stage of crop weed competition. Crops should not be exposed to moisture deficit stress at their critical growth stages.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 8, p.82

chunks.en: Use NPK fertilizers as per the soil test recommendation. Avoid imbalanced use of fertilizers. Use micronutrient mixture after sowing based test recommendations. Do not apply any micronutrient mixture after sowing without test recommendations.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, rows 9-10, p.83

chunks.en: Install pheromone traps at appropriate period. Do not store the pheromone lures at normal room temperature (keep them in refrigerator).
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 12, p.83

chunks.en: Release parasitoids only after noticing adult moth catches in the pheromone trap or as pheromone trap or as per field observation.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 13, p.83

chunks.en: Apply HaNPV or SINPV at recommended dose when a large number of egg masses and early instar larvae are noticed. Apply NPV only in the evening hours after 5 pm. Do not apply NPV on late instar larva and during day time.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 14, p.84

chunks.en: In case of pests which are active during night like Spodoptera spray recommended biocides/ chemicals at the time of their appearance in the night.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 15, p.84

chunks.en: Apply short persistent pesticides to avoid pesticide residue in the soil and produce.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 17, p.84

chunks.en: Follow the recommended procedure of trap crop technology. Do not apply long persistent on trap crop, otherwise it may not attract the pests and natural enemies.
chunks.locator: XIII. Do's and Don'ts in IPM, row 18, p.84

chunks.en: Dimethoate (organophosphate insecticide); classification as per insecticide rules: highly toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: yellow; WHO classification of hazard: Class II moderately hazardous. Symptoms of poisoning: mild-anorexia, headache, dizziness, weakness, anxiety, tremors of tongue and eyelids, miosis, impairment of visual acuity. Treatment of poisoning: for extreme symptoms of OP poisoning, injection of atropine (2-4 mg for adults, 0.5-1.0 mg for children) is recommended. Repeated at 5-10 minute intervals until signs of atropinization occur. Waiting period from last application to harvest (days): printed as '--'.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 1, p.85

chunks.en: Carbofuran (carbamate insecticide); classification as per insecticide rules: extremely toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: red; WHO classification of hazard: Class I b highly hazardous. Symptoms of poisoning: constriction of pupils, salivation, profuse sweating, muscle incordination, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, epigastric pain, tightness in chest. Treatment of poisoning: atropine injection- 1-4 mg. repeat 2 mg when symptoms begin to recur (15-16 min interval) excessive salivation- good sign, more atropine needed. Waiting period from last application to harvest (days): printed as '--'.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 2, p.85

chunks.en: Imidacloprid (neonicotinoid); classification as per insecticide rules: highly toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: yellow. First aid measures: have person sip a glass of water if able to swallow. Do not induce vomiting unless told to do so by a doctor, do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person. Symptoms of poisoning: harmful if swallowed, absorbed through skin or inhaled. Avoid breathing vapor or spray mist. Causes moderate eye irritation. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 3 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 3, p.86

chunks.en: Thiamethoxam (neonicotinoid). First aid measures: have person sip a glass of water if able to swallow. Do not induce vomiting unless told to do so by a poison control center or doctor. Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 5 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 4, p.86

chunks.en: Novaluron (insect growth regulator). First aid measures: have person sip a glass of water if able to swallow. Do not induce vomiting unless told to do so by a poison control center or doctor. Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious. Symptoms of poisoning: causes substantial but temporary eye injury. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 1-3 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 5, p.86-87

chunks.en: Flubendiamide (anthranilic diamide); classification as per insecticide rules: slightly toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: green; WHO classification of hazard: unlikely produce acute hazard. Treatment of poisoning: treat symptomatically as there is no known specific antidote. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 5 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 6, p.87

chunks.en: Indoxacarb (other classes insecticides). First aid measures: have person sip a glass of water if able to swallow. Do not induce vomiting unless told to do so by a doctor. Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person. Symptoms of poisoning: altered blood chemistry. Abnormal decrease in number of red blood cells (anaemia) which could produce tiredness, rapid heartbeat, dizziness, pale skin, leg cramps, shortness of breath, Central nervous system effects. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 5 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 7, p.87

chunks.en: Captan (fungicide); classification as per insecticide rules: moderately toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: blue; WHO classification of hazard: Class III slightly hazardous. Symptoms of poisoning: headache, palpitation, nausea, vomiting, flushed face, irritation of nose, throat, eyes and skin etc. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 6 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 8, p.88

chunks.en: Mancozeb (fungicide); classification as per insecticide rules: slightly toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: green; WHO classification of hazard: unlikely produce acute hazard. Symptoms of poisoning: headache, palpitation, nausea, vomiting, flushed face, irritation of nose, throat, eyes and skin etc. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest: 10 days.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 9, p.88

chunks.en: Copper oxychloride (fungicide); classification as per insecticide rules: moderately toxic; colour of toxicity triangle: blue; WHO classification of hazard: Class III slightly hazardous. Symptoms of poisoning: headache, palpitation, nausea, vomiting, flushed face, irritation of nose, throat, eyes and skin etc. Treatment of poisoning: no specific antidote. Treatment is essentially symptomatic. Waiting period from last application to harvest (days): printed as '--'.
chunks.locator: XIV. Safety parameters in pesticide usage, table, row 10, p.88

chunks.en: Purchase: Purchase only just required quantity e.g. 100, 250, 500, 1000 g/ml for single application in specified area. Do not purchase leaking containers, loose, unsealed or torn bags. Do not purchase pesticides without proper/approved labels. While purchasing insist for invoice/bill/cash memo.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, A. purchase, p.89

chunks.en: Storage: Avoid storage of pesticides in house premises. Keep only in original container with intact seal. Do not transfer pesticides to other containers. Never keep them together with food or feed/fodder. Keep away from reach of children and livestock. Do not expose to sunlight or rain water. Do not store weedicides along with other pesticides.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, B. storage, p.89

chunks.en: Handling: Never carry/ transport pesticides along with food materials. Avoid carrying bulk pesticides (dust/granules) on head shoulders or on the back.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, C. handling, p.89

chunks.en: Precautions for preparing spray solution: Use clean water. Always protect your nose, eyes, mouth, ears and hands. Use hand gloves, face mask and cover your head with cap. Use polythene bags as hand gloves, handkerchiefs or piece of clean cloth as mask and a cap or towel to cover the head (Do not use polythene bag contaminated with pesticides).
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, D. precautions for preparing spray solution, p.89

chunks.en: Read the label on the container before preparing spray solution. Prepare the spray solution as per requirement. Do not mix granules with water. Concentrated pesticides must not fall on hands etc. while opening sealed container. Do not smell pesticides.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, D. precautions for preparing spray solution, p.89

chunks.en: Avoid spilling of pesticides while filling the sprayer tank. Do not eat, drink, smoke or chew while preparing solution. The operator should protect his bare feet and hands with polythene bags.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, D. precautions for preparing spray solution, p.89

chunks.en: Equipment: Select right kind of equipment. Do not use leaky and defective equipment. Select right kind of nozzles. Don't blow/clean clogged nozzle with mouth. Use old tooth brush tied with the sprayer and clean with water. Do not use same sprayer for weedicide and insecticide.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, E. equipment, p.89

chunks.en: Precautions for applying pesticides: Apply only at recommended dose and dilution. Do not apply on hot sunny day or strong windy condition. Do not apply just before the rains and after the rains. Do not apply against the windy direction.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, F. precautions for applying pesticides, p.89-90

chunks.en: Emulsifiable concentrate formulations should not be used for spraying with battery operated ULV sprayer. Wash the sprayer and buckets etc. with soap water after spraying. Containers buckets etc. used for mixing pesticides should not be used for domestic purpose. Avoid entry of animals and workers in the field immediately after spraying. Avoid tank mixing of different pesticides.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, F. precautions for applying pesticides, p.90

chunks.en: Disposal: Left over spray solution should not be drained in ponds or water lines etc. throw it in barren isolated area if possible. The used/empty containers should be crushed with a stone/stick and buried deep into soil away from water source. Never reuse empty pesticides container for any other purpose.
chunks.locator: XV. Basic precautions in pesticides usage, G. disposal, p.90

chunks.en: It is advisable to use protective clothing, face mask and gloves while preparing and applying pesticides. Do not apply pesticides without protective clothing and wash clothes immediately after spray application. Do not apply in hot or windy conditions.
chunks.locator: XVII. Operational, calibration and maintenance guidelines in brief, items 4-5, p.92

chunks.en: Do not smoke, chew or eat while undertaking the spraying operation. Operator should take proper bath with soap after completing spraying. Do not blow the nozzle with mouth for any blockages. Clean with water and a soft brush.
chunks.locator: XVII. Operational, calibration and maintenance guidelines in brief, items 7-9, p.93

uncertain.en: The photo does not show the problem clearly enough for a reliable answer. Take a clearer photo of one affected leaf in daylight, or show the plant to your local KVK or agriculture officer.
uncertain.hi: इस फोटो से भरोसेमंद जवाब नहीं मिल पा रहा है। दिन की रोशनी में एक प्रभावित पत्ती की साफ फोटो लें, या पौधा अपने नज़दीकी कृषि विज्ञान केंद्र (KVK) या कृषि अधिकारी को दिखाएं।

expert_confirm.en: Please confirm this with your local KVK or agriculture officer before spraying anything.
expert_confirm.hi: कोई भी छिड़काव करने से पहले अपने नज़दीकी KVK या कृषि अधिकारी से इसकी पुष्टि कर लें।

chemical_rule.en: The spray options below are copied from ICAR, NIPHM and TNAU publications. Use only one product, follow the label, observe the waiting period before harvest and wear protective clothing. Confirm with your KVK or agriculture officer if unsure.
chemical_rule.hi: नीचे दिए छिड़काव विकल्प ICAR, NIPHM और TNAU के प्रकाशनों से लिए गए हैं। सिर्फ एक दवा इस्तेमाल करें, लेबल के निर्देश मानें, कटाई से पहले की प्रतीक्षा अवधि का पालन करें और सुरक्षा कपड़े पहनें। संदेह हो तो अपने KVK या कृषि अधिकारी से पुष्टि करें।

estimated_severity.en: Estimated spread on the photographed leaf: {level}. This is a rough estimate from the photo colours.
estimated_severity.hi: फोटो वाली पत्ती पर अनुमानित फैलाव: {level}। यह फोटो के रंगों से लगाया गया मोटा अनुमान है।

too_small.en: The photo is too small. Move closer to the leaf.
too_small.hi: फोटो बहुत छोटी है। पत्ती के पास जाकर फोटो लें।

too_dark.en: The photo is too dark. Take it in daylight.
too_dark.hi: फोटो बहुत अंधेरी है। दिन की रोशनी में फोटो लें।

too_bright.en: The photo is too bright. Avoid direct sun or flash on the leaf.
too_bright.hi: फोटो बहुत ज़्यादा चमकीली है। पत्ती पर सीधी धूप या फ्लैश से बचें।

too_blurred.en: The photo is blurred. Hold the camera still and focus on one leaf.
too_blurred.hi: फोटो धुंधली है। कैमरा स्थिर रखें और एक पत्ती पर फोकस करें।

not_an_image.en: The file could not be read as a photo.
not_an_image.hi: यह फाइल फोटो के रूप में नहीं खुल सकी।

pest_species_uncertain.en: An insect was found on the photo, but its exact type is not certain.
pest_species_uncertain.hi: फोटो में एक कीट मिला है, लेकिन उसकी सही पहचान पक्की नहीं है।
